overview: Alutiiq/Sugpiaq homelands extend across coastal south-central Alaska, including Prince William Sound, the outer Kenai Peninsula, Kodiak and the Alaska Peninsula. Archaeology, community knowledge, language records and living artists reveal a continuing maritime culture. The examples here chiefly concern Kodiak, rather than every community across this broad region.

periods.title: Art preserved at Karluk One
periods.summary: Museum collections from Karluk One include painted wooden objects assigned to approximately 1400 to 1750. They preserve evidence of skilled carving, pigments and images of animals and the landscape. This is an archaeological example from Kodiak, not a founding date for all Alutiiq people.

periods.title: Russian coercion on Kodiak
periods.summary: The Russian assault at Awa’uq in 1784 broke Kodiak communities’ political autonomy. Traders took hostages and compelled work, including hunting and food preparation. Communities survived under this colonial system.

periods.title: American rule and pressure on language
periods.summary: After Alaska passed to United States rule in 1867, mission and secular schools imposed English and punished Alutiiq speech. Families faced pressures that disrupted transmission of their language between generations.

periods.title: Rebuilding coastal villages
periods.summary: Earthquake-generated tsunamis devastated Kodiak communities in 1964. Afognak residents relocated to the new community of Port Lions, while Old Harbor families rebuilt. Displacement did not end their community relationships.

periods.title: Teaching and creating for new generations
periods.summary: Kodiak Alutiiq organizations and tribal groups developed language revitalization projects from 2002. Recorded lessons, community teaching and contemporary art connect new work with ancestral knowledge.

items.text: At Nikllirtuusqaq on Karluk Lake, excavators found a deeply dug house with a stone-lined entrance and central hearth. Notched pebble net weights and fish-cleaning knives were common finds. The museum presents the site with camps of roughly 1,300 years ago, interpreting the houses and work areas as places repeatedly used for autumn fishing.

Seven small blue-schist adzes from Nikllirtuusqaq have differently shaped cutting edges. Researchers suggest they could have belonged to a carver’s tool set. The tools establish woodworking at the camp; their ownership as one set remains an interpretation. An engraved pebble also bears a design resembling parka decoration.

A different Karluk Lake house, dated to about 3,000 years ago, contained fishing equipment and traces of household life. Its destruction by fire preserved fragments of woven matting. The charred material adds evidence of furnishings that usually decay; the report does not identify an attacker or establish why the fire began.

A ciqlluaq combined an excavated floor, timber framework, split driftwood boards and insulating sod. Related women and their families shared a central room for cooking, sewing, repairing tools and receiving visitors, with side rooms for sleeping and storage. As frame houses spread, older sod buildings could remain places for bathing, food preparation and gatherings.

Bentwood boxes required carefully prepared planks bent into sides, joined with lashings or fasteners and fitted to a separate base. Small containers carried food and supplies in kayaks. The museum distinguishes this known construction from the exact Alutiiq steaming method, which was not recorded; a documented Tlingit technique cannot simply be assigned to Alutiiq makers.

A painted wooden box panel from Karluk One, dated around 1550, depicts an erupting volcano. Other pieces include a miniature skin-working board showing an otter. Artists prepared colors from plants and crushed minerals mixed with binders. These surviving surfaces show that everyday wooden objects could also carry carefully composed images.

Catalog UAM:EH:0568-5577 describes an adze from Karluk whose maker fastened a metal rasp blade to a wooden handle with cotton cord. The object shows a familiar tool form made with introduced materials. Charles Lucier collected it around 1952; that collection date does not establish when it was manufactured.

At Awa’uq, a refuge off Sitkalidak Island, families sought protection in a naturally defensible place. Russian traders attacked with cannon in 1784, killed many people and took hostages. The museum identifies this massacre as the loss of Kodiak Alutiiq political autonomy, not the disappearance of Alutiiq society throughout its wider homeland.

The Russian settlement at Three Saints Bay relied on Alutiiq hostages forced to hunt and prepare food. When traders moved their settlement to Kodiak in 1793, the Native community remained. Its subsequent movements form part of Old Harbor’s history, which also includes families arriving from other villages after epidemics and later disruptions.

The 1964 earthquake and tsunamis destroyed much of Afognak village. Residents evacuated and established Port Lions in nearby Settler Cove; families entered new houses that December. The move involved creating homes and community infrastructure after a disaster, while carrying relationships and village history into a new location.

Mission and secular schools under American rule punished children for using Alutiiq, sometimes physically. The museum explains how this pressure affected parents’ decisions about teaching the language at home. Reduced transmission was shaped by coercive institutions, while later community teaching projects sought to make public speaking and learning possible again.

The museum’s language archive describes Joe Kelly’s interviews with Larry Matfay about sod-house construction, Deborah Robinson’s interviews with speakers from several villages, and recordings from the 2003 to 2007 master-apprentice project. These collections connect language with biographies and practical knowledge. Their catalog descriptions identify the contributors; they are not substitutes for listening to the recordings.

In 2024 the museum selected oil lamps by Rolf Lee Christiansen made from cobbles gathered below Refuge Rock. One has a carved face designed to emerge as its oil burns. It also selected Cheryl Lacy’s beaded mask How Big Was Your Fish?, which reworks older mask forms through beadwork rather than wood carving.

ending.text: Alutiiq/Sugpiaq communities continue across their homeland. Russian violence brought colonial domination on Kodiak, and later schools and displacement caused further losses. Community institutions, language projects and living artists carry knowledge forward. The map’s 1500 cutoff is a coverage boundary, not the end of these people.
